quotes.t: Even if you have three or four extra syllables-or as many as five or seven-you need not worry as long as the verse sounds right.
quotes.c: Miscellaneous quotations, From a letter to Takayama Biji, 20 June 1682, as quoted in Basho: The Complete Haiku (2013) by Jane Reichhold

quotes.t: Every day is a journey, and the journey itself is home.
quotes.c: Oku no Hosomichi - The Narrow Road to the Interior (1702), Translation of Sam Hamill, Narrow Road to the Interior and other writings (2000), page 3 Seek not the paths of the ancients; Seek that which the ancients sought.

quotes.t: He who creates three to five haiku poems during a lifetime is a haiku poet. He who attains to completes ten is a master.
quotes.c: Miscellaneous quotations, As quoted in Collected Haiku Theory, eds. T. Komiya & S. Yokozawa, Iwanami, 1951 (Unknown translator)

quotes.t: I feel lonely as I gaze at the moon. I feel lonely as I think about myself, and I feel lonely as I ponder upon this wretched life of mine. I want to cry out that I am lonely, but no one asks me how I feel.
quotes.c: Miscellaneous quotations, Basho: The Complete Haiku (2013), Jane Reichhold

quotes.t: It rains during the morning. No visitors today. I feel lonely and amuse myself by writing at random. These are the words: Who mourns makes grief his master. Who drinks makes pleasure his master.
quotes.c: Miscellaneous quotations, Robert Hass (1994) The Essential Haiku: Versions of Bashō, Buson, and Issa

quotes.t: It was a rainy day when I crossed over the Hakone Barrier, and all the mountains were veiled in clouds. Days like this, when Mt Fuji cannot be seen For the misty rain, Have an appeal all on their own.
quotes.c: Miscellaneous quotations, The Literature of Mt Fuji: Japanese Classical Literature, 2017, Chuo University; cited as being from "Nozarashi kiko 野ざらし紀行（Bleached Bones in the Field, 1684)" This haiku also translated by Jane Reichhold in Basho: The Complete Haiku (2013) as: misty showers the day one cannot see Mount Fuji it is more attractive

quotes.t: Moon almost full I'm thirty-nine a child still.
quotes.c: Individual poems, Translation of David Young, Moon Woke Me Up Nine Times: Selected Haiku of Basho (2013)

quotes.t: My body, now close to fifty years of age, has become an old tree that bears bitter peaches, a snail which has lost its shell, a bagworm separated from its bag; it drifts with the winds and clouds that know no destination. Morning and night I have eaten traveler's fare, and have held out for alms a pilgrim's wallet.
quotes.c: Miscellaneous quotations, Genjūan no Fu ("Prose Poem on the Unreal Dwelling") in Donald Keene, Anthology of Japanese Literature, p. 374 (Translation: Donald Keene)

quotes.t: The fact that Saigyō composed the poem that begins, "I shall be unhappy without loneliness," shows that he made loneliness his master. He also wrote: In the mountain village who are you calling, yobuko-bird? I thought you lived alone.:There's nothing so intriguing as living alone.
quotes.c: Miscellaneous quotations, Robert Hass (1994) The Essential Haiku: Versions of Bashō, Buson, and Issa

quotes.t: The haiku that reveals seventy to eighty percent of its subject is good. Those that reveal fifty to sixty percent, we never tire of.
quotes.c: Miscellaneous quotations, As quoted in Collected Haiku Theory, eds. T. Komiya & S. Yokozawa, Iwanami, 1951 (Unknown translator)

quotes.t: やがて死ぬ けしきは見えず 蝉の声 yagate shinu keshiki wa miezu semi no koe
quotes.c: Individual poems, Soon to die yet showing no sign the cicada's voice

quotes.t: 京にても 京なつかしや 時鳥 kyou nitemo kyou natsukashi ya hototogisu
quotes.c: Individual poems, Even in Kyōto- hearing the cuckoo's cry- I long for Kyōto Robert Hass (1994) The Essential Haiku: Versions of Bashō, Buson, and Issa Bird of time - in Kyoto, pining for Kyoto. Basho, On Love and Barley: Haiku of Basho, London, 1985, p. 43 (Translation: Lucien Stryk)

quotes.t: 古人の跡を求めず，古人の求めしところを求めよ。 kojin no ato wo motomezu, kozjin no motometaru tokoro wo motomeyo
quotes.c: Miscellaneous quotations, Seek not the paths of the ancients; Seek that which the ancients sought. Translation found in Jackson, B. (2014) The Inspirational Atheist: Wise Words on the Wonder and Meaning of Life, where it is cited as being from "Words by a Brushwood Gate"

quotes.t: 古池や 蛙飛び込む 水の音 furu ike ya kawazu tobikomu mizu no oto
quotes.c: Individual poems, The old pond: A frog jumps in,- The sound of the water. Classical Japanese Database, Translation #64 (Translation: Reginald Horace Blyth) At the ancient pond the frog plunges into the sound of water (Translation: Sam Hamill) Old pond, leap-splash - a frog. Basho, On Love and Barley: Haiku of Basho, London, 1985, p. 58 (Translation: Lucien Stryk) Breaking the silence Of an ancient pond, A frog jumped into water - A deep resonance. Matsuo Bashō, The Narrow Road to the Deep North and Other Travel Sketches, London, 1966, p. 9 (Translation: Nobuyuki Yuasa)

quotes.t: 夏草や 兵どもが 夢の跡 natsukusa ya tsuwamonodomo ga yume no ato
quotes.c: Oku no Hosomichi - The Narrow Road to the Interior (1702), The summer grasses- For many brave warriors The aftermath of dreams. Donald Keene, Travelers of a Hundred Ages, New York, 1999, p. 316 (Translation: Donald Keene) The summer grasses- Of brave soldiers' dreams The aftermath. Matsuo Bashō, The Narrow Road to Oku, Tokyo, 1996, p. 87 (Translation: Donald Keene)

quotes.t: 旅に病で 夢は枯野を かけ廻る tabi ni yande yume wa kareno wo kake-meguru
quotes.c: Individual poems, Sick on a journey, my dreams wander the withered fields. Bashō's last poem, written while he was dying of a stomach illness. (Translation: Robert Hass) Sick on a journey - over parched fields dreams wander on. Basho, On Love and Barley: Haiku of Basho, London, 1985, p. 81 (Translation: Lucien Stryk) Travelling, sick My dreams roam On a withered moor. (Unknown translator) Reported as Basho's death poem.

quotes.t: 朝顔に 我は飯食ふ 男かな asagao ni ware wa meshi kû otoko kana
quotes.c: Individual poems, I am one Who eats his breakfast, Gazing at morning glories. The Way of Silence: The Prose and Poetry of Basho (1970), Richard Lewis

quotes.t: 行く春や 鳥啼き魚の 目は泪 yuku haru ya tori naki uo no me wa namida
quotes.c: Oku no Hosomichi - The Narrow Road to the Interior (1702), Spring passes and the birds cry out-tears in the eyes of fishes Matsuo Bashō, Narrow Road to the Interior and other writings, Boston, 2000, p. 4 (Translation: Sam Hamill) Spring is passing by! Birds are weeping and the eyes Of fish fill with tears. Matsuo Bashō, The Narrow Road to Oku, Tokyo, 1996, p. 23 (Translation: Donald Keene)

quotes.t: 静けさや 岩に滲み入る 蝉の声 shizukesaya iwa ni shimiiru semi no koe
quotes.c: Oku no Hosomichi - The Narrow Road to the Interior (1702), How still it is! Stinging into the stones, The locusts' trill. Donald Keene, World Within Walls: Japanese Literature of the Pre-Modern Era, 1600-1867, New York, 1999, p. 89 (Translation: Donald Keene)
